paras: The threatened lynching of the Atkins brothers took place near Choctaw City and at Oklahoma City, Oklahoma Territory, at the end of July and beginning of August 1895, after "We" Atkins, a Black laborer, and one or two of his brothers were arrested and charged with the murder of Mrs. J. F. Mitchell. Crowds demanded the prisoner and made "numerous threats of lynching," and twenty-five deputies were reported guarding the men before "We" Atkins was moved to El Reno for safe keeping. White papers in Oklahoma, Kansas and beyond carried the case, most treating the accused's guilt as likely, while the fullest local account doubted the report that the woman had been sexually assaulted.

J. F. Mitchell and his wife lived on a farm about six and a half miles northwest of Choctaw City, where a "colored family by the name of Adkins" occupied a second house, farmed part of the land and had contracted to clear 30 or 40 more acres. According to the Oklahoma City Times-Journal account printed in the Wichita Daily Eagle, Mitchell had knocked "We" Adkins down in a quarrel a few weeks earlier, and Adkins was said to have threatened to get even.

Mrs. Mitchell was killed while walking home alone along a pasture road from a neighbor's house, and her husband, back from work at Choctaw City, organized a search that found her lying face down in the field. The Times-Journal account described a heavy blow from a club to the back of the neck, while a wire dispatch from Oklahoma City spoke of a head wound and marks on her throat. Adkins had been grubbing near the road she took, and after a neighbor brought news of the murder and said bloodhounds would be brought, he set off through a cornfield and was captured by a neighbor about a mile from home.

Taken before a justice for a preliminary hearing, he became the subject of a dispute when Deputy Sheriff Cannon and Deputy Marshals Hopkins and Gault demanded the prisoner and Constable Dobbs claimed him, and the hearing was put off. Two of his brothers were then arrested and held with him at Choctaw City, and the Guthrie Daily Leader reported that "three negroes" were under arrest there, charged with "outraging and killing" Mrs. Mitchell.

In the Times-Journal's words, "the people are greatly wrought up," demands were made that the prisoner be turned over to them, and squads of horsemen were seen heading toward Choctaw City. The same account said that only "absolute certainty that they had the right man" was lacking for the crowd to "take the law in their own hands." On August 2 the Guthrie Daily Leader reported that "We" Atkins and a brother had been jailed at Oklahoma City, that there were numerous threats of lynching, and that twenty-five deputies were required to guard them.

Mrs. Mitchell's funeral, held on a Wednesday, was largely attended, and the preliminary examination of "the Atkins boys" was set for August 20. By August 4 "We" Atkins had been removed from the Oklahoma City jail to El Reno "for safe keeping." No report of the examination, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage through September 1895.

The case ran in white papers of Oklahoma, Kansas, Kentucky and Texas during the first week of August 1895, mostly as short items. The Weekly Call of Topeka printed an Oklahoma City dispatch under the headline "A Terrible Crime," calling the killing "one of the most fiendish and dastardly crimes ever committed in Oklahoma Territory" and saying circumstantial evidence pointed "very strongly" to Atkins's guilt, though he denied it. A one-line wire item in the Maysville, Kentucky, Daily Public Ledger named the suspect "Watkins" and added that he "may be lynched."

The fullest account, the Times-Journal narrative in the Wichita Daily Eagle, laid out the case against Adkins, including the earlier quarrel, a reported attempt to buy a revolver and his flight, yet stated that the report of ravishment was "not verified by the evidence." The Guthrie Daily Leader and the Fort Worth Gazette's "Territory Notes" reported the arrests, the guard and the transfer in brief notes without comment. No Black-press coverage was found, and the only racial terms in the white reports, "colored" and "negroes," were applied to the accused.

Reports differed on how many men were held: one wire item named a single suspect, the Guthrie Daily Leader counted first three and then "Atkins and brother," the Times-Journal account described Adkins and two brothers, and the Fort Worth Gazette said two. Wire items placed the killing on "Monday night" and "At Oklahoma City," a dispatch dated July 31 said "last night" and sixteen miles west of Oklahoma City, and the Times-Journal placed the farm northwest of Choctaw City.

The Topeka dispatch said torn-up ground showed she had fought for "her honor," and the Fort Worth Gazette said she was choked to death, whereas the Times-Journal account found her clothing undisturbed and no evidence of a struggle. The victim appears as Mrs. J. F. Mitchell in most reports and as Mrs. Louisa C. Mitchell in the Fort Worth Gazette, and the accused's surname as Atkins, Adkins and Watkins.
